name: Classical Alternatives Cheaper
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Moving Target: How Classical Computing Keeps Outrunning Quantum Claims
lesson.summary: Repeatedly, problems once thought to require a quantum computer have been solved just as well and far more cheaply by better classical algorithms or raw GPU power, an informal pattern researchers call dequantization.
lesson.body:
One of the clearest reasons genuine paying customers have not materialized, building on the previous chapter, is that classical computing is not a static target quantum computing is racing past. It is a moving target that keeps improving in parallel, and it starts from an enormous head start in cost, reliability, and software maturity. Classical alternatives, ordinary CPUs, GPUs, specialized ASICs, and clever algorithmic techniques like tensor networks and simulated annealing, are already cheap to rent at massive scale and integrate seamlessly into decades of existing enterprise software.

The pattern has a name in the research community: dequantization. When a quantum algorithm is proposed with a claimed speedup on some specific, well-defined problem, researchers frequently go on to discover a classical algorithm, often directly inspired by studying how the quantum approach worked, that matches its performance without needing any quantum hardware at all. The most well-known example concerns quantum algorithms proposed for recommendation-system problems: in 2018, researcher Ewin Tang showed that a purely classical algorithm could match the performance previously thought to require a quantum computer for that class of problem, given similar sampling assumptions. That single result reshaped how seriously the field treats claimed quantum speedups on similar linear-algebra-flavored problems, since it demonstrated that an apparent quantum advantage can sometimes reflect a gap in classical algorithm design rather than a fundamental limit of classical computation.

The cost comparison reinforces the point. Renting GPU time on mainstream cloud platforms typically costs from well under a dollar to a few dollars per hour depending on the hardware tier, and that infrastructure is mature, reliable, and already wired into the software stacks most businesses run. Specialized quantum hardware access, by contrast, remains comparatively expensive per task and requires new expertise, new software tooling, and tolerance for noisy, probabilistic results. When an organization evaluates a real production workload against both options, the classical alternative is very often cheaper, more reliable, and equal to or faster than the quantum option today, which makes the purchasing decision straightforward even for organizations that remain genuinely excited about quantum computing's long-term potential.

This connects directly to the earlier comparison of quantum and classical computing as general-purpose tools: quantum computers are not faster classical computers, they are a fundamentally different kind of machine that offers proven advantages only for a specific, currently narrow set of problems, factoring large numbers and simulating certain quantum systems being the clearest theoretically grounded examples. Outside that narrow set, classical hardware, backed by decades of engineering maturity and constantly improving algorithms, keeps winning on the metrics that matter to a paying customer: cost, reliability, and time to a usable answer.

None of this means quantum computing will never gain a decisive, commercially relevant edge. It does mean the list of problems where quantum computing wins today, in practical and economic terms rather than in a carefully chosen laboratory benchmark, is much shorter than promotional materials tend to suggest, and that list has to keep clearing a bar that classical computing keeps raising.
